text: Recent research suggests that adaptive feedback can improve academic writing when students revise with explicit criteria. This paragraph reviews several sources but reports them in an informal and inconsistent way. Smith 2020 found that peer review increased revision depth, while Chen and Liu observed a similar effect in engineering writing classes. Another study by Martinez showed that automated comments may reduce surface errors when the comments are connected to examples. However, the paragraph does not distinguish narrative citation from parenthetical citation, and it places publication years directly after names without parentheses. The discussion also mentions several findings without page numbers or a reference pattern that readers can verify. Although the content is relevant to educational technology, the citation practice makes the evidence difficult to trace. A reader can understand the general argument, but cannot reliably identify which claim belongs to which source or whether the author follows APA conventions. This limitation is useful for testing whether the system can bind feedback to citation-norm nodes rather than giving only generic advice.

The paragraph argues that online formative assessment improves students' motivation and self-regulation. It introduces a classroom study and then states that Zhang, 2021 proved the value of immediate feedback. It also says that Brown & Wilson, 2019 described a similar pattern in blended courses, but the citation form changes again when the author writes according to Lee 2022, delayed feedback may still be effective. These references are placed inside the sentence without a consistent author-date format. The paragraph then lists three practical implications but does not connect them to specific sources. The wording suggests that all cited studies produced the same conclusion, even though the studies may have used different contexts and methods. The draft therefore needs a traceable citation structure. Each empirical claim should be attached to a verifiable source, and multiple references should be formatted in a consistent style so that the reader can separate literature evidence from the writer's own interpretation.

This study examines how graph-based retrieval can support academic feedback in undergraduate writing. The draft uses several Chinese standard references in the discussion but does not provide enough bibliographic cues. It writes that previous research [1] found higher feedback acceptance and that later research [2] confirmed the pattern, yet the paragraph never explains the author, title, year, or document type associated with those numbers. A reader who only sees this paragraph cannot decide whether the evidence comes from a journal article, conference paper, or course report. The paragraph also switches between numbered citation markers and informal author mentions, such as Wang stated that structured comments were more useful. Because the citation scheme is mixed, the relation between claims and sources becomes weak. The paragraph needs a stable GB/T-style or APA-style reference strategy, and every numbered citation should correspond to a complete reference entry in the bibliography. This sample therefore checks whether feedback can identify both numbering problems and missing bibliographic traceability.

The draft explains that writing analytics can identify weak argumentation patterns and support targeted revision. It then claims that most systems improve students' final scores by more than ten percent, but this statistical claim has no citation. The next sentence cites Johnson and Park for a general description of learning dashboards, while the following sentence says that knowledge graphs are widely used in educational recommendation without naming a source. The paragraph therefore mixes supported and unsupported claims. The problem is not only punctuation or reference style; the stronger problem is that high-impact claims are not anchored to specific evidence. Readers cannot check whether the percentage improvement comes from a controlled experiment, a survey, or a speculative review. The paragraph should cite the empirical source immediately after the quantitative claim, avoid presenting broad claims as established facts, and use a consistent author-date format for every literature-based assertion. The case is designed to test whether the system distinguishes formatting advice from evidence-support advice.

The paragraph summarizes literature on automated essay scoring and intelligent tutoring. It states that early systems focused on grammar, later systems focused on discourse, and recent systems integrate large language models. The draft places one citation at the end of the entire paragraph, such as (Miller, 2023), even though the paragraph contains at least three historical claims. This creates a citation scope problem. The reader cannot know whether the single citation supports all three stages, only the final stage, or merely the general topic. The paragraph also uses several phrases such as studies have shown and researchers believe without specifying which researchers or which studies. A more rigorous version would divide the literature review into smaller evidence units. Each claim about a development stage should be connected to a relevant source, and the final synthesis sentence should clarify what the writer concludes from the cited studies rather than hiding multiple claims behind one broad reference.

The abstract begins by describing a prototype system and immediately reports that the platform was implemented with a graph database, a retrieval module, and a feedback interface. It then states that the system achieved stable streaming responses during testing. Only after these implementation details does the abstract mention that undergraduate students often struggle to connect writing feedback with explicit academic norms. The order makes the abstract difficult to follow because the research problem appears after the solution and results. The paragraph also omits a concise statement of the research objective before describing the technical architecture. Readers encounter many components but do not know what question the system is designed to answer. A clearer abstract should first introduce the educational problem, then state the objective, then summarize the method, and finally report evaluation evidence. The current version contains useful information, but its section logic does not match a conventional problem-method-result-contribution sequence.

This introduction presents several features of an academic writing assistant, including login, session history, citation checking, and visual knowledge graph display. It explains how users can click buttons and receive feedback, but it does not establish the research gap that motivates these features. The paragraph reads like a product description rather than an introduction to a thesis. It does not explain why existing teaching tools are insufficient, why traceable feedback matters, or what specific problem the proposed system addresses. The structure therefore lacks the common introduction movement from background to problem to gap to contribution. The reader sees what was built before understanding why it should have been built. A stronger version would first describe the difficulty of norm-based academic writing feedback, then identify limitations in generic LLM feedback, and finally introduce the proposed GraphRAG binding approach as a response to that gap. The sample should trigger feedback about missing motivation rather than interface wording alone.

The method section says that participants revised their abstracts after receiving system feedback. It then discusses the average score improvement and explains why the treatment group performed better. After that, it returns to describe how the query set was constructed and how the threshold for reference validation was selected. This sequence mixes method and result content. Readers need to know the data source, preprocessing steps, model configuration, comparison groups, and evaluation metrics before they encounter outcome interpretation. When result claims appear inside the method section, the study design becomes harder to reproduce and the boundary between procedure and finding becomes unclear. The section should separate implementation details from experimental outcomes. A revised structure would describe dataset preparation, system configuration, validation procedure, and metric calculation in the method section, while score changes and group comparisons should be moved to the results section. This query checks both IMRAD order and paragraph-role consistency.

The results section describes the user interface and gives a long explanation of why the design is meaningful for teaching. It states that the dashboard provides access to several modules and that the workbench can display retrieved evidence, but it does not report quantitative or qualitative findings from the evaluation. The section title promises results, yet the paragraph mostly repeats implementation details and design rationale. It does not include pass rates, latency values, traceability statistics, or examples from the query set. As a result, the reader cannot determine whether the system met its evaluation goals. The paragraph should be reorganized so that the results section reports evidence produced by the experiment. Interface descriptions can appear in the system design chapter, while this section should present measured outcomes such as node existence rate, threshold pass rate, feedback structure completion, and comparison against baseline methods. The feedback should point to missing results, not merely suggest stylistic polishing.

The conclusion repeats that the system integrates a knowledge graph, retrieval, and a language model. It then introduces a new argument that the platform may reduce teacher workload across all writing courses. This claim has not been tested in the preceding sections, and no deployment evidence is reported. The paragraph also omits limitations. It does not mention that the current evaluation uses a fixed query set, that participant data are only preliminary, or that the knowledge graph still needs expert expansion. A conclusion should synthesize established findings rather than introduce unsupported claims. It should also identify constraints that affect interpretation. The current structure overstates the contribution and leaves readers uncertain about what was empirically demonstrated. A stronger conclusion would summarize the verified traceability results, discuss boundaries of the experiment, and define future work without presenting untested deployment claims as completed evidence. This item tests whether the system flags overgeneralization in the closing section.

The paragraph is intended to provide background for a study on traceable feedback, but it moves directly into implementation details. It says that the system uses a Redis store, a streaming endpoint, and a front-end workspace layout. These details may be useful in a system design section, yet they do not help readers understand the educational background. The paragraph does not explain why students have difficulty applying writing norms, why feedback needs evidence, or why generic comments are insufficient for revision. Because the background function is missing, the paragraph feels disconnected from the research motivation. It should first establish the broader instructional context, such as the need for explicit norm-based academic writing support, and only then transition to the technical response. Without that function, the reader receives technical information before understanding the problem space that makes the design necessary. The case should retrieve background-function norms rather than technical architecture norms.

This paragraph should explain the research method, but it mainly evaluates the quality of the results. It says that the proposed approach is reliable, that the generated feedback is clearer than baseline feedback, and that students can benefit from the system. These statements may belong in a result or discussion section, but they do not describe how the experiment was conducted. The paragraph does not identify the query set, comparison methods, threshold values, annotation process, or scoring procedure. As a method paragraph, it should enable another researcher to reproduce the evaluation. The current wording instead asks readers to accept conclusions without procedural evidence. A revised version should specify how writing snippets were selected, how the four methods were run, how reference IDs were validated, and how pass rates were calculated. Interpretive claims should be moved to a later section after the evidence is presented. This item is useful for detecting absent procedural detail in method writing.

The paragraph presents several results but does not make the function of each sentence clear. It first states that the full GraphRAG method had a higher validation pass rate. It then says that traceable feedback is important for student trust. The next sentence explains how node expansion works, and the final sentence claims that teachers can use the system in class. These sentences mix result reporting, theoretical interpretation, method explanation, and practical implication. The reader cannot identify the main result or understand how the supporting details relate to it. A result paragraph should begin with the measured finding, provide relevant numbers or comparisons, and then briefly interpret what the result indicates. Technical mechanism should be handled in the method section, and broad classroom implications should be reserved for discussion. The current paragraph needs a clearer topic sentence and a consistent result-reporting function. The expected feedback should locate the sentence-level role shifts.

This discussion paragraph reports that the proposed method improved reference validation. It then repeats the numerical result and lists the same pass rate again. The paragraph does not explain why the improvement occurred, what it means for traceability, or how it relates to the limitations of direct LLM generation. A discussion paragraph should interpret findings rather than merely restate them. It should connect the result to the research question and identify possible mechanisms or constraints. For example, it could explain that graph expansion helps retrieve norm nodes that are semantically adjacent to the draft problem, while binding validation filters unsupported reference tags. The current paragraph lacks that interpretive function. It gives the reader the outcome but not the reasoning needed to understand the contribution, so the discussion remains descriptive and underdeveloped. The sample is intentionally focused on interpretive depth rather than citation punctuation. It also checks whether feedback can recommend explanation without inventing new experimental data.

The paragraph is supposed to describe a limitation, but it turns into a promotional statement. It says that the system is scalable, convenient, and suitable for many writing courses. It briefly mentions that the query set is limited, but immediately claims that the current evidence is enough to show broad teaching value. This weakens the limitation function. A limitation paragraph should clearly state what the study cannot prove, explain why the limitation matters, and indicate how future work can address it. In this case, the paragraph should acknowledge that synthetic and fixed evaluation snippets cannot establish classroom learning effects, and that real participant studies require consent, anonymization, and blind scoring. By replacing limitation analysis with positive claims, the current paragraph may mislead readers about the strength of the evidence. The case helps test whether limitation feedback remains cautious and evidence-bound. It should lead to advice about narrowing claims rather than expanding conclusions.

This study investigates a traceable feedback mechanism for undergraduate academic writing. The introduction first describes the difficulty students face when applying citation and structure norms during revision. It then identifies a limitation of generic large language model feedback: comments may be fluent but not always linked to explicit normative evidence. To address this problem, the study proposes a knowledge-graph-based retrieval and binding workflow. The method section explains how writing snippets are processed, how candidate norm nodes are retrieved, and how generated reference tags are validated against node existence and cosine similarity. The evaluation compares a no-retrieval baseline, a vector-retrieval baseline, a no-expansion ablation, and the full GraphRAG method. Results are reported through node existence rate, threshold pass rate, feedback structure completion, and sensitivity analysis over the validation threshold. The conclusion summarizes verified traceability improvements and notes that classroom effectiveness requires later participant studies. The paragraph is included as a no-issue control for false-positive measurement.

The abstract presents a coherent summary of the project. It begins by identifying the instructional problem that students often receive feedback without clear reference to academic writing norms. It then states the objective of designing a teaching assistant platform that combines retrieval, knowledge graph nodes, and large language model generation. The method is described in a compact way: the system retrieves candidate nodes, generates structured feedback, and validates reference tags before returning them to the interface. The abstract also reports the planned evaluation dimensions, including traceability metrics, threshold sensitivity, and comparison with baseline retrieval strategies. It avoids making claims about learning gains because participant deployment is still preliminary. The paragraph closes by stating the expected contribution as a more transparent feedback workflow for academic writing revision. The order follows a problem, method, evaluation, and contribution sequence, and no obvious citation or structural issue is present. This control checks whether the system can avoid unnecessary correction.

The method paragraph is organized around reproducibility. It states that the evaluation uses a fixed set of synthetic and de-identified writing snippets covering citation format, section structure, paragraph function, and control cases. It explains that each query is run under four conditions: no retrieval, vector retrieval, vector retrieval with binding validation, and full GraphRAG with graph expansion and binding validation. The paragraph defines the validation rule as node existence in the knowledge graph and cosine similarity above a selected threshold. It also explains that sensitivity analysis is conducted by recalculating pass rates under multiple threshold values. The paragraph does not interpret results before describing the procedure. Instead, it gives readers enough information to understand how outputs will be generated and checked. This method function is clear, and the paragraph maintains a stable procedural focus from beginning to end. It is therefore suitable for measuring false-positive correction behavior. No participant identity or private classroom information is included.

The results paragraph reports evaluation findings in a bounded way. It first states that traceability is measured by the proportion of generated references that correspond to existing knowledge graph nodes and pass the similarity threshold. It then explains that comparison tables should present the four methods under the same query set so that the effect of graph expansion and binding validation can be separated. The paragraph avoids claiming that students learned more from the system because the current dataset is designed for system validation rather than causal teaching evaluation. It also notes that low-confidence references should be counted as degraded outputs rather than silently accepted. The function of the paragraph is consistent: it defines what kind of result is meaningful for RQ2 and how those results should be interpreted. The text is traceable, focused, and does not mix method description with unsupported classroom conclusions. It should normally require no corrective feedback.

The conclusion paragraph synthesizes the expected scope of the study without overstating the evidence. It explains that the platform demonstrates how large language model feedback can be connected to explicit norm nodes through retrieval and post-generation validation. It states that the main empirical support comes from traceability metrics on a fixed writing snippet set and from threshold sensitivity analysis. The paragraph also recognizes limitations: the current data do not prove long-term learning gains, and future classroom deployment should collect consent-based drafts and blind rubric scores. The conclusion therefore separates system verification from educational effectiveness. It identifies the contribution as a transparent feedback workflow rather than a completed proof of instructional impact. This paragraph has a clear concluding function, refers back to the research objective, and avoids introducing new unsupported claims after the evaluation has ended. It is a control case for cautious conclusion writing. The system should avoid marking this balanced limitation statement as problematic.
